meta.title: Who really said "Politicians are like diapers. They need to be changed regularly, and for the same reason"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Robin Williams said a version on screen in 2006 — he didn’t write it. Quote Investigator traces the diaper joke to a 1966 newspaper column.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Politicians are like diapers. They need to be changed regularly, and for the same reason'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Robin Williams and not Mark Twain. Quote Investigator finds the diaper version in print in 1966, forty years before the movie line.

answer.label: Not Robin Williams — an anonymous joke he made famous
answer.authorDates: Earliest close match located by Quote Investigator: Dick Nolan’s column, The San Francisco Examiner, 10 November 1966
answer.sourceLine: Robin Williams spoke a version of this line on screen in Man of the Year (2006), but he did not write it — the film was written and directed by Barry Levinson, and Williams’s character introduces the gag as an old, anonymous phrase. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the diaper form back to a Dick Nolan column in The San Francisco Examiner of 10 November 1966, and finds the joke evolved from an older simile about changing socks; no single originator is documented.

source.excerpt: our rulers ought to be changed routinely, like diapers for the same reason
trail: 10 September 1952 — the sock ancestor. A letter in the Boston Traveler runs “Office holders, like socks, should be changed often and for very much the same reason,” per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗. A politicians-and-socks version follows in The Indianapolis Star in 1958.

10 November 1966 — diapers, in print. Dick Nolan’s San Francisco Examiner column carries the earliest close match QI could locate ↗. The joke then recurs unattached: a Fort Thomas council candidate in October 1987, a bumper sticker reported by The Wall Street Journal in 1991.

1 May 1992 — the campaign-trail version. Tom Blair’s San Diego Union-Tribune column prints congressional candidate John Wallner’s wording, the closest ancestor of today’s phrasing; the Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ follows it from there into Reader’s Digest and Paul Harvey’s syndicated commentary.

13 October 2006 — the movie. Robin Williams delivers it in Barry Levinson’s Man of the Year, prefacing it as an old anonymous phrase. The Twain credit appears only afterwards, which is why every fact check — Gigafact’s included ↗ — answers “no.”
source.excerptNote: Dick Nolan, The San Francisco Examiner, 10 November 1966 — described by Quote Investigator ↗ as the earliest close match it located. Nolan writes it into his own commentary on political turnover; he credits no one, and QI credits no single originator for the diaper version.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for this wording, because no author or first publication has been identified: Quote Investigator ↗ traces it as an evolving folk joke and credits no originator. The documented forms that do have owners are all modern and in copyright — the 1966 Nolan column, the 1992 Tom Blair column, and Barry Levinson’s 2006 Man of the Year screenplay — so nothing here supports treating the line as public domain.

author.name: Robin Williams
author.heading: The man who made it famous — but didn’t write it
author.bio: Robin Williams was born in Chicago on 21 July 1951 and began performing stand-up in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1976, starting out at the Holy City Zoo. He became famous for improvisational speed — in Good Morning, Vietnam he was allowed to play the role without a script — which is part of why lines he merely delivered are so often mistaken for lines he invented. The diapers joke is one of those: he said it as Tom Dobbs in Barry Levinson’s Man of the Year (2006), and the Center for Mark Twain Studies calls him “the man most responsible for the popularity the aphorism now enjoys” — a very different claim from authorship. Williams died on 11 August 2014.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with no author and four famous claimants. The two that dominate search results are Robin Williams, who said a version out loud in a movie, and Mark Twain, who was dead for more than half a century before the diaper form is documented in print.

items.why: Williams delivers the line as Tom Dobbs in Man of the Year (2006), a film written and directed by Barry Levinson ↗ and released on 13 October 2006. The character explicitly frames the gag as “an old phrase, basically anonymous” before telling it — the movie is disclaiming authorship inside the scene that made it famous. The Center for Mark Twain Studies calls Williams “the man most responsible for the popularity the aphorism now enjoys” ↗, which is a claim about spread, not about origin.

Quote Investigator states flatly that “There is no substantive evidence that Mark Twain who died in 1910 said or wrote this joke” ↗, and the Center for Mark Twain Studies could find no instance of the line being attributed to Twain until roughly two years after the 2006 film. The Twain label is younger than the movie it came from.

Columnist Tom Blair printed Wallner’s version in the San Diego Union-Tribune on 1 May 1992: “Politicians are like diapers. They both should be changed often. And for the same reason.” It is the closest match to today’s wording, but Quote Investigator ↗ documents the diaper joke in print in 1966, 1987 and 1991, so Wallner was passing along a joke already in circulation.

items.who: George Bernard Shaw, Benjamin Franklin, Eça de Queirós
items.why: Lead Stories notes the same line has been incorrectly attributed to Shaw, Franklin and the Portuguese writer Eça de Queirós ↗ as well — the classic signature of an ownerless joke looking for a name.

misattribution.truthLine: No one owns it. The earliest close match located by Quote Investigator ↗ is a Dick Nolan column in The San Francisco Examiner of 10 November 1966, and QI concludes the jest “evolved over time from a humorous simile about changing socks” — crediting no single originator and noting that earlier instances may yet turn up.

context.heading: How a sock joke became a diaper joke
lead: The gag is older than its punchline. Quote Investigator’s chronology starts with a family of similes about socks: a letter printed in the Boston Traveler on 10 September 1952 ran “Office holders, like socks, should be changed often and for very much the same reason,” and The Indianapolis Star carried a politicians-and-socks version in 1958. Swapping socks for diapers made the unstated reason cruder and funnier, and the joke stopped needing to explain itself.

The diaper form shows up in a Dick Nolan column in The San Francisco Examiner on 10 November 1966, then circulates the way jokes do — a 1987 city-council candidate in Fort Thomas, Kentucky; a 1991 bumper sticker noted in The Wall Street Journal; a 1992 congressional candidate quoted in a San Diego newspaper column. It had been public property for decades before any famous name was attached to it.
detailsBody: The 1992 instance is the one most often mistaken for the origin. Columnist Tom Blair printed it in the San Diego Union-Tribune on 1 May 1992 as “Politicians are like diapers. They both should be changed often. And for the same reason,” from Libertarian congressional candidate John Wallner — whose repeated use of it during a losing 1992 campaign got it into several major papers, including the Los Angeles Times, which called it “the best line in a losing cause.” Quote Investigator’s earlier citations show Wallner was reusing an existing joke, not minting one.

The Mark Twain credit is the newest layer, not the oldest. The Center for Mark Twain Studies could find no instance of the line being attributed to Twain until roughly two years after Man of the Year opened — which means the “19th-century wisdom” framing arrived after the 21st-century movie.
context.pull: The film that made it famous introduces it as “an old phrase, basically anonymous.”
